title: Youth health is improving on some emotional and dietary indicators while sleep, activity, and digital-risk constraints persist
source_unit: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Youth Health in Focus release; national Youth Risk Behavior Survey data for 2023–2025 and 10-year trends for 2015–2025
geography: United States; nationally representative high school student estimates

denominator.unit: national YRBS high school student estimate universe

observations.method: CDC national Youth Risk Behavior Survey estimates summarized in the Youth Health in Focus release.
observations.uncertainty: The measures are survey estimates and the release highlights selected statistically significant differences; the cross-sectional series does not establish why the indicators changed or whether gains will persist.
observations.counterinterpretation: Improvement in population indicators does not mean distress has resolved, that every subgroup improved equally, or that school, family, community, and public-health interventions caused the change.

denominator.unit: national YRBS high school student estimate universe

observations.method: CDC national Youth Risk Behavior Survey estimates summarized in the Youth Health in Focus release.
observations.uncertainty: These are descriptive population changes and do not identify changes in household food access, school meals, prices, sports availability, or other mechanisms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Better reported dietary indicators and sports participation do not imply that overall physical activity, nutrition quality, or health equity improved across all students.

denominator.unit: national YRBS high school student estimate universe

daily_physical_activity_and_guideline_me.unit: CDC reported trend status from 2023 to 2025

daily_physical_education.unit: CDC reported trend status from 2023 to 2025

observations.method: CDC national Youth Risk Behavior Survey estimates and trend summary.
observations.uncertainty: The release reports population-level trend status but does not identify whether sleep and activity constraints arise primarily from schedules, built environments, school policy, family conditions, health, or technology use.
observations.counterinterpretation: A stable or low population share is not proof that every student experiences inadequate sleep or that physical education alone would resolve the constraint.

observations.period: 2023–2025; U.S. high school students with relevant behavior

text_or_email_while_driving.unit: percent of students who drove in the past month; 2025 and 2023

observations.method: CDC national Youth Risk Behavior Survey estimates summarized in the Youth Health in Focus release.
observations.uncertainty: The release reports associations and trend indicators, not causal effects of social media or digital communication on sleep, safety, nutrition, or mental health.
observations.subgroup: U.S. high school students; driving measure limited to students who drove in the past month.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stable social-media frequency does not establish stable exposure intensity, content, platform mix, or individual harm; the driving measure does not explain why students text while driving.

boundary: This record captures CDC-reported national changes in selected youth mental-health, dietary, activity, sleep, and digital-behavior indicators. It does not establish causal mechanisms, subgroup equity, intervention effects, or future persistence.
